**PARIS, France (CNN) —** In a city renowned as the birthplace of the avant-garde, keeping pace with the latest trends can be a challenge. Here is a rough guide to what is hot right now in the French capital.

### Tecktonik

This beat is Tecktonik, the latest dance craze to hit the streets of Paris. Parisian youths love their trends, and Tecktonik—a fusion dance style typically accessorized with spiked hair and neon accessories—is sweeping the city. Look out for groups of young people dancing outside the Trocadéro. You may even be lucky enough to catch a Tecktonik-versus-breakdance dance-off.

### Le Scrapbooking

Scrapbooking is the current craze among Paris’s more sedate residents. Visit Le Temple Du Scrap (13 Rue Ernest Cresson) for pretty paper supplies, trimmings, ribbons, and all manner of related frippery.

### Bike Around Town

Much of Paris is walkable, but Vélib’, the city’s inexpensive bike-hire scheme launched in 2007, makes getting around even easier. Thousands of bicycles are available at stations across the city, spaced approximately 300 meters apart. The first 30 minutes of each journey are free, and you will need a credit card to register for the scheme.

Once you have your bike, you are ready to career through the cobbled streets of Montmartre and rattle along the Seine.

### Café Hotspots

The classic Parisian image of smoky cafés has now been banished to the pavements, thanks to a smoking ban in bars and restaurants introduced at the end of 2007. *Quel dommage!*

In winter, the hottest spots in café culture are those with heated terraces. You can still light up while sipping a *petit café crème*, but only if you sit outside—so bring a turtleneck and a beret to stay warm as well as stylish.

### Massages at the Mosque

Paris is home to a large Muslim population, and La Grande Mosquée de Paris (Rue Geoffroy St. Hilaire) reflects that heritage. The building is absolutely stunning from the outside and even more spectacular within.

Treat yourself to a massage at the hammam, or Turkish bath, and you could easily imagine yourself in Morocco. Afterward, relax with a mint tea in the courtyard. Be sure to check in advance which days are reserved for men and which are for women.

### Subway Style

Taking the subway in Paris can be a drag. Striking drivers and filthy platforms can make the Métro a miserable experience. Yet the light at the end of this often dark and dingy tunnel is the Palais Royal–Musée du Louvre stop—more specifically, the Palais Royal entrance.

Like so many things in Paris, it is a work of art in its own right, created by French artist Jean-Michel Othoniel. His design, featuring brightly colored glass beads, is a delight. Nearby Place Colette is also an excellent spot for people-watching: pull up a pew and enjoy.

### Paris in Fashion: From Tecktonik to Hammams

Paris has always balanced tradition with experimentation, and its urban trends reflect that mix. Alongside historic cafés, elegant boulevards, and famous monuments, the city continually develops new ways to dance, travel, socialize, and relax. Recent crazes—from Tecktonik and scrapbooking to bicycle sharing and hammam treatments—offer a lively portrait of a capital where youth culture, practical innovation, and multicultural traditions coexist.

One of the most visible youth phenomena is Tecktonik, an energetic dance style associated with electronic music. Dancers perform rapid, angular arm movements, often combining them with quick footwork and dramatic poses. The style grew through clubs, public gatherings, and online videos, becoming as much a fashion statement as a form of dance. Tight jeans, brightly colored accessories, futuristic graphics, and carefully styled hair helped create a recognizable Tecktonik identity. In parks, squares, and nightclubs, young Parisians turned the dance into a public display of creativity and belonging.

A quieter but equally enthusiastic trend is scrapbooking. Participants arrange photographs, ticket stubs, handwritten notes, decorative paper, and other keepsakes into personalized albums. Although the activity has strong international influences, Parisian enthusiasts have adapted it to their own tastes, often incorporating images of the city, vintage typography, fashion motifs, and souvenirs from everyday life. Workshops and specialty shops allow beginners to learn techniques and exchange materials. In a fast-moving digital world, scrapbooking offers a tactile way to preserve memories and transform ordinary experiences into carefully designed objects.

Innovation is also visible in the way Parisians move around the city. The Vélib bicycle-sharing system has made cycling a practical alternative to cars, taxis, and crowded public transportation. With rental stations distributed across Paris, users can collect a bicycle in one neighborhood and return it in another. The service encourages short journeys, reduces dependence on automobiles, and allows residents and visitors to experience the capital at street level. Cycling past markets, gardens, and riverside paths can reveal details that are easily missed from inside a métro carriage. Although traffic and limited bicycle availability can present challenges, Vélib has become an important symbol of greener urban living.

Parisian café culture, meanwhile, continues to adapt without losing its traditional character. Heated terraces allow customers to sit outside even during colder months, extending the familiar ritual of drinking coffee, reading, talking, and watching pedestrians go by. These terraces preserve the café’s role as an extension of public life: neither entirely indoors nor fully part of the street. They also demonstrate how an old Parisian institution can respond to changing habits while maintaining the atmosphere that makes it distinctive.

For relaxation, the hammam at the Grand Mosque of Paris offers a very different experience. Inspired by North African bathing traditions, the hammam provides a warm, steam-filled environment where visitors can unwind, cleanse their skin, and receive treatments such as exfoliation or massage. The surrounding complex, with its Islamic architecture, decorative tiles, garden, and tearoom, reflects the deep cultural connections between France and the Muslim world, particularly North Africa. A visit can therefore be both restorative and culturally enriching.

Taken together, these activities reveal several sides of contemporary Paris. Tecktonik represents youthful experimentation and the rapid spread of trends through music and media. Scrapbooking shows a desire for personal creativity and handmade objects. Vélib illustrates the city’s search for sustainable, convenient transportation, while heated terraces preserve the social pleasures of café life. The Grand Mosque’s hammam highlights Paris’s multicultural heritage and its openness to traditions from beyond metropolitan France. Far from being defined only by its monuments and history, Paris remains a city that constantly absorbs new influences and reinvents everyday life.

# Paris beyond the postcards: Dance floors, paper crafts and a city best explored on two wheels

**Paris, France** — The Eiffel Tower still sparkles, the Seine still draws sunset crowds and café terraces remain the city’s unofficial living rooms. But Paris is also a place of constantly recycled trends, where early-2000s dance culture can reappear on social media, traditional paper crafts find a new generation and public bicycles offer one of the most rewarding ways to move between neighborhoods.

Here’s how to experience a more playful, creative side of the French capital.

## Tecktonik’s electric afterlife

Tecktonik — the frenetic French dance style recognized by windmilling arms, sharp gestures and an electro soundtrack — exploded in the Paris suburbs and clubs during the 2000s. Its spiked hair and neon uniforms are no longer a dominant street look, but the movement’s influence survives in electro nights, dance battles and online revival culture.

Travelers hoping to catch that energy should look beyond fixed “Tecktonik shows” and check current listings for electro parties, freestyle dance events and open-air sessions. Clubs around eastern Paris, warehouse venues on the city’s fringes and summer gatherings along the Seine and canals are the most likely places to encounter dancers blending Tecktonik-era moves with voguing, hip-hop and contemporary club styles.

The appeal is less about nostalgia than reinvention: Parisian dance culture rarely lets a good movement disappear completely.

## Scrapbooking, the Parisian way

In a city devoted to beautiful paper, scrapbooking feels less like a hobby and more like an extension of everyday life. Stationery stores sell patterned papers, rubber stamps, fountain pens, decorative tape and notebooks so attractive they can turn a Metro ticket into a miniature work of art.

Creative travelers can assemble a visual diary from café receipts, museum stubs, market labels and vintage postcards found at flea markets. Contemporary paper boutiques such as Papier Tigre offer bold, graphic supplies, while department and craft stores — including Le BHV Marais — are useful stops for tools and materials.

For something more atmospheric, browse the booksellers along the Seine or the stalls of the Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen. Old maps, advertisements and ephemera can provide a distinctly Parisian foundation for a travel scrapbook.

## Vélib’: Paris at handlebar level

Few changes have reshaped sightseeing in Paris as much as Vélib’, the city’s bike-share network. Mechanical and electric bicycles can be picked up and returned at stations across the capital and surrounding communities, making them practical for short journeys as well as leisurely rides.

The most enjoyable routes avoid the busiest traffic. Follow the Bassin de la Villette and Canal de l’Ourcq, ride along protected stretches beside the Seine, or explore the increasingly bike-friendly corridors connecting central Paris with neighborhoods farther east.

Electric Vélib’ bikes make bridges and hillier districts easier, although availability can fluctuate during rush hour. Visitors should review current pricing and access requirements before setting out, inspect the brakes and tires, and remember that Parisian bike lanes can be busy with commuters, scooters and delivery riders.

For many travelers, cycling reveals the scale of the city better than the Metro: grand monuments give way to pocket parks, bakeries and quiet residential streets in a matter of minutes.

## The enduring theater of the café terrace

No trend in Paris has proved more durable than sitting outside with a coffee and watching the city pass. Heated terraces, expanded outdoor seating and pedestrianized streets have made café life even more visible across the capital.

Saint-Germain-des-Prés offers literary associations and classic people-watching, but more contemporary terrace scenes can be found around the Canal Saint-Martin, South Pigalle, Belleville and the Marais. Early mornings belong to regulars with an espresso; afternoons bring laptops and long lunches; evenings turn the pavement into a sprawling social club.

The simplest approach is often the best: choose a busy corner, order a *café crème*, glass of wine or sparkling water, and resist the temptation to rush. A terrace is not merely a place to refuel. It is one of Paris’ essential stages.

## Steam and mint tea at the Grand Mosque

The Grande Mosquée de Paris, near the Jardin des Plantes in the 5th arrondissement, offers a dramatic change of pace. Its Hispano-Moorish architecture, tiled courtyards and garden create one of the city’s most tranquil cultural spaces.

The complex has long been associated with a traditional hammam experience, alongside a restaurant, tearoom and pastry counter. After a steam bath and scrub — where services are operating and available — visitors can linger over sweet mint tea and honeyed North African pastries.

Access rules, opening schedules and service arrangements may change, so travelers should check directly before visiting. Even without a hammam appointment, the mosque’s café and courtyard offer a serene encounter with the North African heritage that is integral to modern Paris.

Visitors should dress and behave respectfully, remembering that this is an active place of worship rather than simply an attraction.

## A jeweled Metro entrance at the Palais Royal

At street level near the Louvre and Palais Royal stands one of Paris’ most unexpected pieces of public art: the **Kiosque des Noctambules**, marking the Palais Royal–Musée du Louvre Metro station.

Created by French artist Jean-Michel Othoniel, the entrance is crowned with two domes of colorful glass beads. One suggests day, the other night; together they resemble an oversized piece of jewelry dropped into the formal architecture of central Paris.

It is a sharp contrast to the city’s famous Art Nouveau Metro entrances and an ideal starting point for a short cultural walk. From here, travelers can cross into the arcades and gardens of the Palais Royal, view Daniel Buren’s striped columns in the courtyard, browse nearby galleries and continue toward the Louvre.

Visit early for clearer photographs, or after dark, when the glasswork takes on a more theatrical glow.

## A city of old habits and new rhythms

Paris’ most interesting trends are rarely entirely new. They emerge through layering: Tecktonik gestures return in a new dance vocabulary, scrapbooks preserve the disposable traces of a trip, and bike lanes redraw routes through centuries-old streets.

The best itinerary connects those layers. Cycle beside the canal, collect paper scraps at a market, pause on a café terrace, unwind near the Grand Mosque and finish beneath the glass beads of the Palais Royal Metro entrance.

In Paris, even the newest scene tends to come with a little history — and even the oldest ritual can feel newly discovered.

## Paris now: a rough visitor’s guide

Paris’s current energy is less about grand boulevards and more about the **10th, 11th, 19th and 20th arrondissements**, plus the inner suburbs of **Pantin and Montreuil**. Think natural wine, specialty coffee, vintage sportswear, run clubs, bouldering, DJ collectives and long evenings beside the canals.

### Youth culture after dark
- **Canal Saint-Martin and the 11th:** waterside drinks, small wine bars and busy terraces around Oberkampf and Parmentier.
- **Belleville and Ménilmontant:** multicultural food, dive bars, artist studios and less-polished nightlife.
- **La Villette and Pantin:** warehouse-style clubs, electronic music and summer spaces along Canal de l’Ourcq.
- Look at **Shotgun** and **Resident Advisor** for that week’s parties. Venues such as **La Station–Gare des Mines, Cabaret Sauvage, Badaboum** and seasonal **Kilomètre25** are useful starting points.
- Vintage shopping remains huge: browse **Guerrisol**, **Kilo Shop** and independent shops around rue Keller, rue de Charonne and the Marais.

Paris nightlife starts late. Bars fill after 9 p.m.; clubs may not peak until 1–2 a.m. Avoid unofficial taxis after closing.

### What locals are doing
- **Running:** Canal Saint-Martin, the Seine quays, Parc des Buttes-Chaumont and Bois de Vincennes. Social run clubs are increasingly popular.
- **Bouldering:** chains such as **Arkose** and **Climbing District** combine climbing with cafés and coworking.
- **Pétanque:** Canal de l’Ourcq, Arènes de Lutèce and neighborhood squares.
- **Roller-skating and cycling:** the Seine’s pedestrianized banks are ideal; organized skate nights sometimes cross the city.
- **Outdoor lounging:** Buttes-Chaumont, Parc de Belleville and Bassin de la Villette feel more local than the central gardens.
- **Flea-market browsing:** Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen for serious hunting; neighborhood brocantes for a more casual experience.

### Coffee and café culture
For classic Paris, order an espresso at the bar rather than settling in with a laptop. For newer coffee culture, try:

- **Ten Belles** – strong specialty-coffee pioneer near Canal Saint-Martin.
- **Dreamin Man** – tiny, carefully made coffee spot.
- **Motors Coffee** – central and coffee-focused.
- **Café d’Auteur** – polished roastery and tasting-room atmosphere.
- **Substance Café** – an intimate coffee experience; check reservations.
- **Café de Flore or Les Deux Magots** – historically significant, photogenic and expensive rather than cutting-edge.

The modern café-bar crossover often involves **natural wine, small plates and vinyl**. In the 11th and 20th, follow busy terraces rather than famous names. Always check current opening days—many independent places close Sunday, Monday or both.

### Wellness, Paris-style
- **Hammam at the Grande Mosquée de Paris:** atmospheric and traditional; verify current hours and gender-specific sessions.
- **Piscine Pontoise:** an Art Deco swimming pool near the Latin Quarter, especially appealing for an early swim.
- **Molitor:** landmark 1930s pool complex with a hotel spa; considerably more luxurious.
- **Yoga or sound-bath studios:** concentrated in the Marais, 9th and 10th; **HOY Paris** is a useful wellness-oriented address.
- **Park reset:** walk barefoot on the lawns where permitted, picnic at Buttes-Chaumont, or take a slow circuit around Lac Daumesnil.
- **Bath and spa splurge:** hotel spas at the Cheval Blanc, Lutetia and Hôtel de Crillon offer high-end treatments, often bookable by non-guests.

### Getting around
- The **Métro** is usually fastest; buses are better for sightseeing.
- Load tickets or passes onto a **Navigo Easy** card or use the official **Île-de-France Mobilités** app. Fare products have changed recently, so confirm current prices there.
- Airport travel uses separate tickets or fares; ordinary central-Paris tickets may not cover it.
- **Vélib’** bikes are excellent for short journeys, but inspect brakes and tires before releasing a bike. Electric bikes disappear quickly at rush hour.
- Google Maps works well, while **Citymapper** is especially useful for Métro exits and disruption options.
- Keep your phone and wallet secured around station doors, ticket machines and crowded lines. Pickpocketing is the main visitor concern.
- Late at night, use official taxis or established ride-hailing apps.

### A stylish Métro architecture tour
Build a self-guided ride around these stations and entrances:

1. **Abbesses** – one of the best-known surviving Hector Guimard Art Nouveau entrances.
2. **Arts et Métiers** – Line 11’s platforms resemble a copper-clad submarine.
3. **Louvre–Rivoli** – museum-style displays and a dramatically renovated interior.
4. **Concorde, Line 12** – walls spell out the *Declaration of the Rights of Man* in letter tiles.
5. **Palais Royal–Musée du Louvre** – the colorful “Kiosque des Noctambules” entrance by Jean-Michel Othoniel.
6. **Cité** – deep platforms, globe lights and an almost theatrical approach to Île de la Cité.
7. **Franklin D. Roosevelt** – sleek, contemporary lighting and design.
8. **Bir-Hakeim** – less about the station than the elevated Line 6 views toward the Eiffel Tower.
9. **Line 14 stations** – spacious, automated and distinctly modern compared with the century-old network.

Also look for original **Guimard entrances**, white beveled tiles, old ceramic station signs and the elegant elevated viaducts of Line 6.

### An easy one-day “current Paris” route
Start with coffee near **Canal Saint-Martin**, walk northeast along the water to **Bassin de la Villette**, then explore **Buttes-Chaumont** and **Belleville**. Have dinner in the 11th or 20th, followed by a natural-wine bar or an electronic-music event. The next morning, recover with a swim, hammam or slow café breakfast before taking the architecture-focused Métro loop.

The key rule: reserve headline restaurants, but leave room for spontaneous neighborhood discoveries—the most fashionable Paris is often one street beyond the place everyone already knows.

# Paris, Now

Paris in the late 2000s is loosening its collar. The grand boulevards still gleam, but the city’s fashionable energy has shifted toward design hotels, natural wine bars, art spaces and canalside cafés. Here’s how to enjoy the capital at its most current.

## Check In

Book a room at **Hôtel Amour** in the 9th, where artist-designed interiors and a leafy courtyard attract a creative crowd. For an edgier address, **Mama Shelter** brings Philippe Starck style, communal tables and rooftop energy to the 20th arrondissement.

## Browse

Start at **Colette** on rue Saint-Honoré, the era’s definitive concept store: fashion upstairs, limited-edition trainers below and a famous water bar in the basement. Then visit **Merci**, the Marais newcomer mixing clothes, furniture, books and café culture beneath a glass roof.

## Look

The **Palais de Tokyo** is the essential stop for contemporary art without the museum hush. Its raw concrete spaces, late opening hours and adventurous exhibitions make it feel closer to a cultural laboratory than an institution.

For photography, cross the river to the **Maison Européenne de la Photographie** in the Marais.

## Lunch

Order tea, salad and a slice of carrot cake at **Rose Bakery**, the Anglo-French canteen that helped make organic simplicity chic. If you can secure a table, **Le Comptoir du Relais** offers generous bistro cooking with serious culinary credentials.

## Stroll

Follow the **Canal Saint-Martin**, where iron footbridges, shabby-chic boutiques and crowded waterside pavements provide a relaxed alternative to Saint-Germain. Pick up bread, cheese and a bottle of wine for an impromptu picnic beside the locks.

Or borrow a grey **Vélib’** bicycle—the city’s new shared-bike sensation—and ride from the Bastille to the Seine.

## Sip

Paris has finally discovered the proper cocktail. Slip through the discreet doorway of the **Experimental Cocktail Club** for carefully mixed drinks in a dark, intimate room. Later, try **Le Baron**, the tiny former brothel near the Champs-Élysées where fashion insiders, musicians and models gather after midnight.

## Dine

Seek out the new generation of compact, chef-led restaurants. **Frenchie**, tucked into rue du Nil, serves inventive market cooking in a room that feels informal but ambitious. For natural wine and small plates, explore the bars around the 10th and 11th arrondissements, where the city’s neo-bistro movement is gathering pace.

## Dance

For velvet-rope glamour, head to **Le Montana** in Saint-Germain-des-Prés. If you prefer music to posing, look east: **La Flèche d’Or**, set in a former railway station, hosts indie bands and late-night parties away from the polished western districts.

## Brunch

The weekend scene belongs to courtyards and communal tables. Return to **Hôtel Amour** for coffee under the foliage, or head to **Mama Shelter** for a lively brunch among DJs, designers and bleary-eyed night owls.

## Finish

End on the steps of **Sacré-Cœur** at dusk, then wander downhill through Pigalle. Neon signs flicker, scooters buzz past and the rooftops stretch toward the horizon—a classic Paris view with the restless energy of a city reinventing itself.

counterfactuals.output:
# What’s Hot in the French Capital

Paris may be celebrated for timeless monuments, but its liveliest pleasures are often found at street level—or just below it.

Start at the **Trocadéro**, where the broad esplanade facing the Eiffel Tower has long attracted young dancers showing off the rapid, angular moves of **Tecktonik**, the electro-dance style born in the Paris club scene. Performances are informal and unpredictable, so weekends and fine-weather afternoons offer the best odds.

For a different kind of cutting and pasting, visit **Le Temple du Scrap**, a specialist shop carrying decorative papers, albums, stamps and tools for scrapbooking. Check its current address and opening hours before setting out, as Paris’s independent craft retailers occasionally relocate or trade online.

To cover more ground, hire one of the sturdy bicycles from **Vélib’ Métropole**, the city’s self-service bike network. Stations are scattered across Paris; a day pass and the Vélib’ app make it easy to pedal along the Seine, through the Marais or beside the Canal Saint-Martin.

Smokers driven outdoors by France’s indoor-smoking ban gather on café terraces across the city. In colder weather, look for a **heated terrace**—particularly around Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Montparnasse or the grands boulevards—where coffee, conversation and cigarettes continue under glowing lamps. Terrace smoking rules and heating policies can change, so follow posted guidance.

For deeper relaxation, head to the **Grande Mosquée de Paris** in the Latin Quarter. Its traditional hammam has historically offered steam baths, exfoliation and massage, often with women-only access. Services and availability vary, making advance confirmation essential. Even without a treatment, the mosque’s tiled courtyard and mint-tea salon are worth the visit.

Finally, don’t rush through the **Métro**. At **Arts et Métiers**, Line 11’s copper-clad platforms evoke the interior of a Jules Verne submarine. **Louvre–Rivoli** displays museum-inspired reproductions, while **Concorde** turns the text of the Declaration of the Rights of Man into a vast typographic mosaic. In Paris, even the commute can be a gallery visit.

counterfactuals.prompt: Pretend you are a CNN travel writer in Paris shortly after the 2007 smoking ban and Vélib launch. Describe six current Paris trends and attractions, with practical locations and advice for tourists.
counterfactuals.output:
## Paris, newly smoke-free—and on two wheels  
*An early-2008 dispatch*

Paris has not abandoned its rituals: the zinc counter, the long lunch, the cigarette held like punctuation. But the city is changing. A smoking ban is clearing café interiors, thousands of rental bicycles are reshaping short journeys, and once-overlooked neighborhoods are drawing visitors away from the monuments. Here are six trends and attractions worth following.

### 1. Join the Vélib revolution

Since its July 2007 debut, Vélib has turned Paris into a vast bicycle-sharing experiment. Gray bicycles wait at docking stations every few blocks, offering an appealing alternative to crowded Métro carriages.

A one-day pass costs about €1 and a seven-day pass €5; the first 30 minutes of each ride are free, after which charges climb quickly. Return the bicycle and take another rather than keeping one all afternoon.

**Where:** Stations are especially plentiful around the Marais, Bastille, Saint-Germain and the Latin Quarter. The Canal Saint-Martin and the Seine embankments make pleasant rides.

**Tourist advice:** The terminals require a substantial card authorization—around €150—and some foreign magnetic-stripe cards may not work. Ask your hotel about compatible cards or nearby staffed rental shops. Avoid the traffic around the Arc de Triomphe, and check that the green return light appears when docking.

### 2. Experience the new smoke-free café

The French smoking restrictions began in public buildings and workplaces in February 2007 and extended to cafés, restaurants, bars and nightclubs on January 1, 2008. For visitors accustomed to emerging from dinner smelling like an ashtray, the difference is remarkable.

The ban has not eliminated Parisian smoking culture; it has pushed it onto terraces, some of which are enclosed or heated. Indoors is now generally the clearer-air choice.

**Where:** Try classic café territory around Boulevard Saint-Germain, Place de la Bastille or Rue Montorgueil.

**Tourist advice:** If smoke bothers you, request an interior table rather than assuming the terrace will be fresher. Smokers should step outside and use the ashtrays provided—fines can apply to both patrons and establishments.

### 3. Discover the Musée du quai Branly

Opened in 2006 near the Eiffel Tower, the Musée du quai Branly is Paris’s most talked-about new museum. Jean Nouvel’s building appears behind a dense garden, while its collections bring together art and cultural objects from Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas.

The dark, winding galleries are atmospheric, though visitors may find the presentation more theatrical than chronological.

**Where:** 37 Quai Branly, 7th arrondissement. Métro: Alma-Marceau; RER C: Pont de l’Alma.

**Tourist advice:** Allow at least two hours and reserve ahead for temporary exhibitions. Combine the museum with a walk beneath the Eiffel Tower or across the Passerelle Debilly to the Palais de Tokyo.

### 4. Trade the Seine for Canal Saint-Martin

Young Parisians are gathering along the Canal Saint-Martin, where iron footbridges, plane trees and green-painted locks provide a relaxed alternative to the grand central boulevards. The area is liveliest around Rue de Lancry, Quai de Valmy and Quai de Jemmapes.

Pick up bread, cheese and wine for a waterside picnic, or continue north to the Bassin de la Villette, where former warehouses now contain cinemas, cafés and cultural spaces.

**Where:** Start near Place de la République and walk north toward Jaurès or Stalingrad. Métro: République, Jacques Bonsergent, Goncourt or Jaurès.

**Tourist advice:** Go in late afternoon and stay for dinner, but keep valuables close when the banks become crowded. The canal is picturesque rather than pristine, so swimming is not an option.

### 5. See Paris become a beach

Every summer, Paris Plages transforms stretches of roadway beside the Seine into an urban resort, complete with sand, deck chairs, games, concerts and temporary cafés. A second major site at the Bassin de la Villette adds boating and waterside activities.

It is less a beach holiday than a demonstration of how eagerly Parisians reclaim space from cars.

**Where:** The principal Seine installation runs along the Right Bank near the Hôtel de Ville; another is at Bassin de la Villette in the 19th arrondissement.

**Tourist advice:** Paris Plages is seasonal, generally operating from mid-July to mid-August, and admission is free. Arrive early for a deck chair, bring sunscreen and do not expect to swim in the Seine.

### 6. Visit Paris’s newest architecture showcase

The Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine, opened in 2007 inside the Palais de Chaillot, offers enormous casts of cathedral façades, models of French buildings and displays on modern architecture. Its scale is surprising, and its windows provide one of the city’s finest views of the Eiffel Tower.

It is particularly useful for travelers who want to understand the buildings they will encounter elsewhere in France—from Romanesque churches to Le Corbusier.

**Where:** 1 Place du Trocadéro, 16th arrondissement. Métro: Trocadéro.

**Tourist advice:** Visit in the morning before the Trocadéro terraces fill with tour groups. Allow about two hours, then walk downhill across the Pont d’Iéna to the Eiffel Tower. Check opening days before setting out; Paris museums commonly close on either Monday or Tuesday.
